But if you know how to add your own weight to the weight of nature, doubling the Mercury and tripling the sulfur, the work will be more quickly finished into a good state, then into a better one, and finally into the best. Although only one sulfur is apparent, there are two Mercuries, but they are of one root; they are neither raw nor over-cooked, yet they are purified and dissolved, if you have understood me.

    There is truly no need to describe the matter of the Mercury of the Philosophers nor the matter of their sulfur. No mortal has been able, nor will be able in the future, to describe it more openly and clearly than it has been described and named by the ancient Philosophers—unless he wishes to be an <term>anathema artis</term> <gloss>an abomination/curse of the art</gloss>. For it is so commonly named that it is even held in low esteem; for this reason, seekers turn themselves toward other subtleties rather than remaining in the simplicity of nature. We do not say, however, that the Mercury of the Philosophers is some common thing and is openly named, but we speak of the matter from 

<summary>Sendivogius explains that while nature can produce results on its own, the alchemist can accelerate the process by balancing the weights of sulfur and mercury. He notes that the true material of the Great Work has already been named by ancient masters, though its common name causes many to overlook its value.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury of the Philosophers, sulfur, weight of nature, alchemical purification, ancient philosophers, simplicity of nature</keywords>
